title: JavaScript Advanced Async Patterns Core Check
description: Check your understanding of generators, async iterators, for await...of, streaming, cancellation, retries, backoff, concurrency limits, queues, debouncing, throttling, and Observables.
author: DailyCoder

questions.prompt: What does `yield` do inside a generator function?

options.text: It sends out a value and pauses the generator
It cancels every Promise in the program
It parses JSON automatically
It makes the function run in parallel

questions.explanation: `yield` produces a value and pauses the generator until the next `.next()` call.

questions.prompt: What does an async iterator's `.next()` method return?

options.text: A Promise that resolves to an iterator result object
Only a string
A synchronous DOM event
A completed array every time

questions.explanation: Async iterator `.next()` calls return Promises for objects such as `{ value, done }`.

questions.prompt: Which syntax consumes an async iterable?

options.text: `for await...of`
`for sync...of`
`await forEach`
`Promise.loop`

questions.explanation: `for await...of` loops over async iterables one value at a time.

options.text: They allow data to be processed gradually as chunks arrive
They make all network requests synchronous
They prevent all possible errors
They require every value to be stored upfront

questions.explanation: Streaming lets code process pieces of data over time instead of waiting for everything first.

options.text: Cancelling async operations that support an abort signal
Converting objects to JSON
Creating private class fields
Sorting Promise results

questions.explanation: `AbortController` creates a signal that supported APIs, such as `fetch()`, can use for cancellation.

questions.prompt: Do JavaScript Promises have built-in cancellation by themselves?

options.text: No, cancellation must be supported by the async operation or API
Yes, every Promise has a `.cancel()` method
Only promises created with `var` can be cancelled
Only fulfilled promises can be cancelled

questions.explanation: A Promise represents a result. Cancellation requires cooperation from the underlying async operation.

options.text: Increasing the delay between retry attempts
Running every retry at the same exact time
Cancelling successful requests
Parsing response headers into arrays

questions.explanation: Exponential backoff spaces retries farther apart after repeated failures.

options.text: To control how many async operations run at the same time
To force all code to become synchronous
To remove the need for error handling
To make arrays immutable

questions.explanation: Concurrency limits prevent too many operations from running at once, which can protect browsers, servers, and APIs.

options.text: An older async result that is no longer relevant when it finishes
A JSON object with missing quotes
A Promise that fulfilled successfully
An array returned from `map()`

questions.explanation: Stale results commonly happen when an older request finishes after a newer request.

questions.prompt: What is an async queue used for?

options.text: Storing tasks and processing them later in a controlled way
Making CSS animations faster
Deleting errors from the console
Replacing every Promise with a callback

questions.explanation: Async queues help manage work that arrives over time and should be processed in order or with limits.

options.text: When work should run after frequent events pause
When every event must run immediately
Only when parsing JSON
Only for class constructors

questions.explanation: Debouncing waits until rapid events settle, such as a user pausing while typing.

options.text: A pattern for values pushed to subscribers over time
A Promise that always resolves once
A browser-only JSON type
A required replacement for `async/await`

questions.explanation: Observables model event-like streams where subscribers receive values over time.
